title: The hotel room standard and why guests judge cleanliness
moduleTitle: Group (Cleaning & Hygiene): Quality, evidence and handover
audience: Cleaners and team members on short-stay, hotel-style and serviced-apartment turnovers, and anyone who checks a room after another person has cleaned it.
learningOutcomes: Describe the parts of a guest-ready room standard: what is seen, touched, smelt and found.
Explain why one visible fault can shape a guest's view of the whole room.
Identify which parts of the standard come from the business's written quality standard and which need a coordinator's decision.

instruction.heading: What a room standard covers
instruction.body: A room standard is the set of conditions a room must meet before the next guest arrives. It is more specific than a general sense that a room is tidy. It covers what a guest sees (surfaces, the bed, the bathroom, the floor), what a guest touches (the points many hands use), what a guest smells, how the air and temperature feel, and whether the supplies a guest expects are in place. Higher-tier accommodation sets the bar higher, because guests arrive with firm expectations and compare rooms closely. A standard only helps when it is written down and applied the same way each time, so that two cleaners given the same room produce the same result.

instruction.heading: Why one small fault changes the whole judgement
instruction.body: Guests rarely inspect a room methodically, but they notice what is out of place. A dusty lamp, a smear on the bathroom mirror or a hair in the basin can lead a guest to wonder what else was missed. The judgement forms quickly, from the points a guest looks at and touches first, and it then colours the rest of the stay and any review that follows. For that reason the cleaner does not treat the parts that are easy to see as the whole job. Every listed point counts, including the ones that are not on a guest's first glance.

instruction.heading: Clean has three parts
instruction.body: In this group a room counts as clean only when three things are true. It looks clean, with no dust, marks or residue on the surfaces a guest sees. It has been treated where it matters, which means high-touch surfaces have been disinfected with a product used as its label directs. And it is neutral in smell and comfortable in temperature. A room can look clean and still fail on touch or smell, so each part is checked separately. The lessons that follow in this group break these three parts into practical steps.

instruction.heading: Where the standard comes from
instruction.body: The standard comes from the business's written quality standard and from any requirements the property sets for itself. The cleanliness of accommodation may also be governed by state or territory law or by local rules. The source article behind this lesson describes state-level rules in a different market, and those rules are not used here. Do not present this lesson as a statement of legal obligation. Where the business or property has a specific standard, that standard governs the job.

procedure: Read the written room standard for the property before starting, including any items the property has listed.
Identify the parts of the standard that apply to this room: seen surfaces, touch points, bed, bathroom, supplies, floor, air and temperature, and final presentation.
Treat any visible fault as a fault in the whole room. Do not accept a room that is clean only where it will be looked at first.
If the standard is unclear, or conflicts with the property's instructions, ask the coordinator before you proceed.
Record the standard you worked to on the job checklist.

workedExamples.situation: A two-bedroom serviced apartment is booked for a family arriving at 3 pm. You start at 9 am. The bed is made and the floor is vacuumed, but a light fitting above the dining table is dusty and the remote control is sticky.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can you mark the room ready because the bed and the floor look right?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The bed and floor are only part of the standard. The dust and the sticky remote are both listed points, so the room is not ready until they are dealt with. Work through the full sequence and the checklist before the room is released.

equipmentAndPpe: Business-issued cloths and buckets, set up for the business's cleaning method
Approved cleaning and disinfectant products, with labels and SDS available
Gloves suited to the products in use
The room standard or job checklist for the property

commonErrors.error: Treating the room as finished when the most visible parts look good.
commonErrors.prevention: Work the full standard, including the points that are not in the first line of sight.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a room is guest-ready because it was cleaned earlier.
commonErrors.prevention: Check every room against the standard, whoever cleaned it last.

commonErrors.error: Using air freshener to cover a smell.
commonErrors.prevention: Find and remove the source first. See “Odour and temperature checks” for odour and temperature checks.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The cleanliness of accommodation may be regulated by law or local rules. Check the rules for the state or territory and the type of accommodation before relying on this lesson for any compliance statement.
Completing this lesson does not qualify anyone to certify a property as compliant with any regulation or inspection standard.

qualityStandard: The room meets every section of the written standard before it is marked ready.
No visible dust, marks or stray items remain on any surface a guest would see or touch.
The cleaner can name each part of the standard and say how it was checked.
documentationEvidence: Completed job checklist showing the standard applied to the room
Photos where the business requires them for the job
summary: A guest-ready room meets a written standard for what is seen, touched, smelt and found.
Small visible faults shape a guest's judgement of the whole room, so every listed point counts.
Clean means visibly clean, treated where it matters, and neutral in smell and temperature.

knowledgeChecks.question: The bed is made and the floor is vacuumed, but a light fitting above the table is dusty. What is the correct conclusion?
options: The room is ready, because the parts a guest sees first look good
The room is not yet ready, because the dust is a listed part of the standard
The room is ready if the dust is removed on the next visit

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a business write its room standard down?
options: So that two cleaners given the same room produce the same result
So that cleaning can be billed at a higher hourly rate
Because a written standard replaces the need to check the room

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about the room standard is correct?
options: A room that smells neutral does not need its touch surfaces cleaned
Standards only apply to rooms that a guest has complained about
A room that looks clean can still fail on smell or touch surfaces
